Google Cloud: a nightly job without my laptop

The problem it solves

Some jobs have to run every day whether or not my laptop is open: scrape a few sites, process the results and push the updates to a web shop. Cron on my own machine fails the first time the machine sleeps. A virtual machine that runs all day for a ten-minute job is a waste, and one more server to maintain.

The general idea

Package the job as a container and let Google Cloud run it only when it is needed. Cloud Run jobs run a container to completion and then stop, so I pay for minutes, not for a server. Cloud Scheduler triggers the job on a cron schedule, and Prefect records every run so I can see what happened. The whole release is a few commands, wrapped in one just recipe.

Examples

A Dockerfile on the Playwright image, which already has the browsers, with dependencies from the lockfile:

FROM mcr.microsoft.com/playwright/python:v1.53.0-jammy
WORKDIR /app
RUN pip install -U pip uv
COPY pyproject.toml uv.lock* ./
RUN uv sync --frozen --no-editable
COPY . .
CMD ["uv", "run", "-m", "myjob.workflow"]

Build, update the job, run it once and schedule it:

gcloud builds submit --tag "$REGION-docker.pkg.dev/$PROJECT/$REPO/$IMAGE:$VERSION"
gcloud run jobs update "$JOB" --image="..." --region="$REGION"
gcloud run jobs execute "$JOB" --region="$REGION"
gcloud scheduler jobs update http "$JOB-daily" \
  --schedule="0 3 * * *" --time-zone="Europe/Budapest" --location="$REGION"

Tips from my setup

  • One word for the whole release. In the Justfile, deploy is build followed by update-job, and release adds update-scheduler. just release is the only command I remember. See the post about just.
  • The same command locally and in the cloud. just run-local and the container both start the same uv run -m entry point, so what works on my laptop works in the job.
  • Reproducible builds. uv sync --frozen installs exactly what the lockfile says, and the image tag carries a version, so I can go back to the previous one.
  • Test before shipping. just test runs pytest, including a test that mimics the workflow.
  • Secrets stay out of git. Keys live in untracked env files and are never committed. A dedicated secret manager is the next step.
  • Observability. Prefect gives every run a history and logs, so a failed night is something I see in the morning, not something I find out from the shop.
